algorithms.title: Binary Search Tree Operations (Search, Insert, Delete)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(H) where H is tree height (O(log N) balanced, O(N) skewed)
algorithms.summary: Core BST dictionary operations: Search, Insert, and Delete node (handling 0, 1, and 2 children with in-order successor replacement).
explanation: 1. BST Property: For every node, all values in its Left Subtree are `< node.val` and all values in its Right Subtree are `> node.val`.
2. Search: Compare key with `node.val`. If `key < node.val` search Left; if `key > node.val` search Right; else found!
3. Insert: Search for insertion position until reaching `null`. Attach new node as leaf.

4. Delete: Locate target node. Case 1 (Leaf): Remove node. Case 2 (1 Child): Replace node with child. Case 3 (2 Children): Find Inorder Successor (min node in right subtree), replace node value with successor value, and recursively delete successor.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Delete Node 5 in BST [5, 3, 6, 2, 4, null, 7]
traceSteps: Target Node to delete is 5 (Root, 2 Children).
Find Inorder Successor: Min node in Right Subtree of 5 is 6.
Replace Root value 5 with Successor value 6.
Recursively delete original node 6 from Right Subtree.
Updated BST root becomes 6 with children 3 and 7.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maintains dynamic ordered set supporting fast search, insertion, and deletion operations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when maintaining dynamically changing sorted data requiring log-time lookups and modifications.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Database indices (B-Trees / Red-Black Trees), C++ std::set / std::map, Java TreeSet.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Prunes half of the search space at each comparison step in balanced trees.

codeTemplates.code:
def deleteNode(root, key):
    if not root: return None
    if key < root.val:
        root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.val:
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key)
    else:
        if not root.left: return root.right
        if not root.right: return root.left
        curr = root.right
        while curr.left: curr = curr.left
        root.val = curr.val
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, curr.val)
    return root

algorithms.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
algorithms.summary: Validates whether a binary tree satisfies the strict Binary Search Tree ordering properties across all subtrees.
explanation: 1. Pitfall: Checking only `root.left.val < root.val < root.right.val` is INSUFFICIENT because right descendants must be greater than all ancestral nodes!
2. Range Validation: Pass valid range `(low, high)` down recursion. Root value must satisfy `low < root.val < high`.
3. Recurse `left` with range `(low, root.val)` and `right` with range `(root.val, high)`.
4. Inorder Traversal Alternative: Inorder traversal of a valid BST must yield a strictly increasing sorted array.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Validate BST on [5, 1, 4, null, null, 3, 6]
traceSteps: Right Child 4: Range (5, +inf) -> Violation! 4 is not > 5.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Verifies correctness of BST invariants after tree modifications or deserialization.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when checking data integrity of search tree data structures.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Database index integrity verifiers, self-balancing tree assertions.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Single pass O(N) traversal validates all subtree invariants simultaneously.

algorithms.title: Kth Smallest and Kth Largest Element in BST
algorithms.summary: Finds the K-th smallest or K-th largest node value in a BST using early-stopping Inorder or Reverse-Inorder traversal.
explanation: 1. Inorder Traversal Property: Inorder traversal (`Left -> Root -> Right`) visits BST nodes in strictly sorted ascending order.
2. Kth Smallest: Perform Inorder traversal. Decrement `k` at each visited node. When `k == 0`, current node is the K-th smallest!
3. Kth Largest: Perform Reverse-Inorder traversal (`Right -> Root -> Left`) visiting nodes in strictly descending order. Decrement `k` until 0.
4. Stop traversal immediately once K-th element is found (Early Exit).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Locates order statistics (K-th minimum / maximum) without array sorting.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when finding rank statistics in BSTs.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Database percentile queries, median streaming algorithms.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Early stopping processes only first K nodes in O(H + K) time rather than O(N) full array sort.

algorithms.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
algorithms.summary: Exploits BST ordering properties to find the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of nodes p and q in O(1) extra space.
explanation: 1. BST Ancestor Rule: If both `p.val` and `q.val` are smaller than `curr.val`, LCA MUST lie in the Left Subtree.
2. If both `p.val` and `q.val` are larger than `curr.val`, LCA MUST lie in the Right Subtree.
3. Split Point: If one value is smaller and one value is larger (or equal to `curr.val`), `curr` is the split point and thus the LCA!
4. Iteration continues until split point is reached.

exampleTrace.title: Trace LCA(p=2, q=8) in BST Root=6 [6, 2, 8, 0, 4, 7, 9]
traceSteps: Split point detected! One value lies left, one lies right.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds lowest shared ancestor in BSTs without hash sets or node parent pointers.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when finding LCA specifically in Binary Search Trees.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Taxonomy classification, version control commit history trees.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Iterative BST property check uses strict O(1) space compared to standard binary tree O(H) stack.

algorithms.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) amortized for next() and hasNext()
algorithms.summary: Implements an iterator over a BST that returns nodes in ascending sorted order using controlled stack-based Inorder traversal.
explanation: 1. Maintain an explicit `stack` of tree nodes representing left-leaning traversal state.
2. Helper `pushAllLeft(node)`: Push `node` and all its left descendants onto stack.
3. Constructor initializes `pushAllLeft(root)`.
4. `next()`: Pop top node `curr` from stack. Call `pushAllLeft(curr.right)` to process right subtree. Return `curr.val`.
5. `hasNext()`: Return `len(stack) > 0`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides controlled step-by-step element streaming over BSTs in sorted order.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when lazy iteration over sorted BST elements is needed without preallocating an array.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Database cursor iterators, streaming data processing pipelines.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Achieves O(1) amortized time per next() query using minimal O(H) stack memory.

algorithms.title: Convert Sorted Array to Height-Balanced BST
algorithms.summary: Constructs a height-balanced BST from a sorted array using divide-and-conquer binary splitting.
explanation: 1. Height-Balanced Constraint: Depth of two subtrees of every node must never differ by more than 1.
2. Divide & Conquer: Pick the middle element `mid = (left + right) // 2` as root.
3. Recursively build Left Subtree from `nums[left ... mid-1]`.
4. Recursively build Right Subtree from `nums[mid+1 ... right]`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Sorted Array [-10, -3, 0, 5, 9]
traceSteps: Left subarray [-10, -3] → Mid is -3 → Left Child = -3.
Right subarray [5, 9] → Mid is 9 → Right Child = 9.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Converts flat sorted arrays into optimal height-balanced search trees.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when building search trees from static sorted datasets.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Static database indexing, fast binary search tree scaffolding.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Splitting at exact middle guarantees logarithmic height O(log N) with minimal depth.

algorithms.title: Inorder Predecessor and Successor in BST
algorithms.summary: Finds the Inorder Predecessor (largest value smaller than key) and Inorder Successor (smallest value larger than key) in a BST.
explanation: 1. Successor Logic: Start at root. If `key < curr.val`, update `succ = curr` and move left. If `key >= curr.val`, move right.
2. Predecessor Logic: Start at root. If `key > curr.val`, update `pred = curr` and move right. If `key <= curr.val`, move left.
3. If target node has a Right Child, successor is the Minimum node in its right subtree.
4. If target node has a Left Child, predecessor is the Maximum node in its left subtree.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Successor of Key 8 in BST [10, 5, 15, 2, 8, 12, 20]
traceSteps: Inspect 10: 8 < 10 → Candidate Succ=10. Move Left to 5.

algorithms.title: Recover Binary Search Tree (Two Swapped Nodes)
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space using Morris Traversal
algorithms.summary: Restores a BST where exactly two node values were swapped by mistake without altering tree structure.
explanation: 1. Inorder Traversal Anomaly: Inorder traversal of a valid BST is strictly sorted.
2. If two nodes are swapped, there will be 1 or 2 places where `prev.val > curr.val`.
3. First Anomaly: `first = prev`, `middle = curr`.
4. Second Anomaly (if non-adjacent): `last = curr`.
5. Swap node values: if `last` exists swap `(first.val, last.val)` else swap `(first.val, middle.val)`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Recover BST [1, 3, null, null, 2]
traceSteps: Swap values of first (3) and last (1).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Fixes corrupted binary search trees in-place when two nodes are misplaced.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when restoring BST invariant without reconstructing the tree.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Database repair tools, memory-constrained tree restoration.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Morris Traversal enables in-place O(N) detection and swap with zero extra stack memory.

algorithms.title: Merge Two Binary Search Trees
algorithms.summary: Merges two BSTs into a single sorted list or balanced BST in O(N + M) linear time.
explanation: 1. Perform Inorder traversal on `root1` to produce sorted array `list1` (size N).
2. Perform Inorder traversal on `root2` to produce sorted array `list2` (size M).
3. Merge two sorted arrays `list1` and `list2` into a single sorted array using Two Pointers in O(N + M).
4. (Optional) Convert merged sorted array into a height-balanced BST in O(N + M).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines data from two independent BSTs into unified sorted output.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when merging search tree database indexes.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Database index merging (LSM-tree compaction), multi-source sorted data aggregation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Two-pointer array merge achieves linear O(N + M) time vs O((N+M) log(N+M)) re-insertion.

codeTemplates.code:
def getAllElements(root1, root2) -> list[int]:
    def inorder(node, lst):
        if not node: return
        inorder(node.left, lst)
        lst.append(node.val)
        inorder(node.right, lst)
    l1, l2 = [], []
    inorder(root1, l1)
    inorder(root2, l2)
    i = j = 0
    res = []
    while i < len(l1) and j < len(l2):
        if l1[i] < l2[j]:
            res.append(l1[i]); i += 1
        else:
            res.append(l2[j]); j += 1
    res.extend(l1[i:])
    res.extend(l2[j:])
    return res

algorithms.title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
algorithms.summary: Finds if there exist two node values in a BST that add up to a target sum K using Dual BST Iterators (Two Pointers).
explanation: 1. Dual Iterator Idea: Standard Two Sum on sorted array uses `left` and `right` pointers.
2. Create Ascending BST Iterator (Left → Root → Right) for `left` pointer.
3. Create Descending BST Iterator (Right → Root → Left) for `right` pointer.
4. Fetch `val1 = leftIter.next()` and `val2 = rightIter.next()`.
5. If `val1 + val2 == K`, return `True`. If `< K`, advance `leftIter`. If `> K`, advance `rightIter`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Two Sum Target=9 on BST [5, 3, 6, 2, 4, null, 7]

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Solves Two Sum on BST in linear time using optimal O(H) stack space.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when finding target sum pairs in Binary Search Trees.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Tree-based sum pair queries, database index joining.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Dual BST Iterator eliminates the need for an O(N) auxiliary array while preserving Two-Pointer traversal.

def findTarget(root, k: int) -> bool:
    def push_left(node, st):
        while node: st.append(node); node = node.left
    def push_right(node, st):
        while node: st.append(node); node = node.right
    st_left, st_right = [], []
    push_left(root, st_left)
    push_right(root, st_right)
    left_node = st_left[-1]
    right_node = st_right[-1]
    while left_node and right_node and left_node != right_node:
        v1, v2 = left_node.val, right_node.val
        if v1 + v2 == k: return True
        if v1 + v2 < k:
            node = st_left.pop()
            push_left(node.right, st_left)
            left_node = st_left[-1] if st_left else None
        else:
            node = st_right.pop()
            push_right(node.left, st_right)
            right_node = st_right[-1] if st_right else None
    return False
